questions.stem: A 27-year-old businessman presented with a 14-day history of watery loose stool, bloating, and some intermittent abdominal pain. Symptoms had started on the day of his return from a 9-day business trip to Thailand. He also noted fat droplets in his stools. He had stayed in a hotel and only ventured out of the hotel on one occasion. He had enjoyed the local food served during his trip and was fond of fresh fruit, salads, and iced drinks.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: Giardia spp. The exposure to iced drinks even in a hotel setting along with fresh salads, likely to have been washed in local water, is suggestive of Giardia infection. The development of symptoms with watery diarrhea at 7–14 days is typical of Giardia infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q8

questions.question: A father and child all present with watery diarrhea. A poor-quality microscopy image is shown (presumably of the organism/trophozoite). [image-based question: poor-quality picture, presumably of organism/trophozoite on microscopy]

parts.text: What is the causative organism?
Treatment?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the causative organism?
B) Treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Giardia lamblia (also called Giardia duodenalis / Giardia intestinalis) — the most commonly identified intestinal parasite; trophozoites show prominent nuclei and clawlike median body on trichrome stain, and clustered person-to-person spread between young children and their parents/siblings is characteristic.
b) Tinidazole 2 g PO as a single dose is the drug of choice (efficacy ~90%). Acceptable alternatives: metronidazole 250 mg PO tid x 5-7 days (efficacy 80-95%); nitazoxanide 500 mg PO bid x 3 days; albendazole 400 mg PO daily x 5 days. Pediatric dosing: tinidazole 50 mg/kg single dose (max 2 g). In pregnancy avoid nitroimidazoles in the first trimester; paromomycin 500 mg tid x 5-10 days may be used.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives metronidazole 500 mg PO BID x 5-7 days; Mandell Table 279.3 lists 250 mg PO tid x 5-7 days, which is followed here.

cohort_answer.text:
Giardia lamblia OR Giardia duodenalis OR Giardia intestinalis
First choice is: Tinidazole 2g PO x 1 dose. Or Nitazoxanide 500mg PO BID x 3 days. Alternative: Metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 5-7 days

a) Giardia lamblia (Giardia duodenalis / Giardia intestinalis) — fits watery diarrhea with intrafamilial spread between young children and parents; diagnosis by stool O&P (3 specimens for >90% sensitivity), stool antigen (85-98% sensitive), or PCR.
b) Tinidazole 2 g PO single dose (drug of choice, ~90% efficacy). Alternatives: metronidazole 250 mg PO tid x 5-7 days (80-95%); nitazoxanide 500 mg PO bid x 3 days; albendazole 400 mg PO daily x 5 days. Pediatric: tinidazole 50 mg/kg single dose (max 2 g). Pregnancy: avoid nitroimidazoles first trimester; paromomycin 500 mg tid x 5-10 days an option.

cohort_answer.text: A) Giardia lamblia. B) First line: Tinidazole 2g PO x1 or Nitazoxanide 500mg PO BID x3 days; Alternate: Metronidazole 500mg PO BID x5-7 days.

An asplenic patient with sepsis after a dog bite.
A necrotizing scalp infection after swimming.

Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite.
Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming.
CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea.

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium septicum (non-traumatic gas gangrene/hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic malignancy, associated with GI/colorectal lesions). b) Capnocytophaga canimorsus - splenectomy is a strong risk factor for this dog-bite/scratch pathogen. c) Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh-water exposure necrotizing soft-tissue infection). d) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) - the classic cause of chronic diarrhea in CVID.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the dog-bite answer (Capnocytophaga canimorsus) is grounded in this chapter; Clostridium septicum, Aeromonas hydrophila, and Giardia are established associations from general Mandell/ID knowledge, not this asplenia chapter.

parts.text: Dog bite -> sepsis

parts_raw.text: Dog bite -> sepsis
Scalp wound cellulitis from fresh water

questions.model_answer: a) Capnocytophaga canimorsus — a slender gram-negative rod with tapered ends inhabiting the canine oral cavity; classic cause of post-dog-bite sepsis, especially in asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or otherwise immunocompromised patients, and may progress to DIC and purpura fulminans. b) Aeromonas hydrophila — wound infection/cellulitis after fresh-water exposure (others to consider: Plesiomonas, Edwardsiella; salt water: Vibrio vulnificus, Shewanella; and Erysipelothrix from fish/animal handling). c) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) — the classic cause of chronic bloating and diarrhea in common variable immunodeficiency. d) Clostridium septicum — atraumatic (spontaneous) myonecrosis with bullous skin lesions and gram-positive bacilli, strongly associated with underlying malignancy (colonic adenocarcinoma, hematologic malignancy/neutropenia).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part (a) is covered in this chapter; (b) Aeromonas, (c) Giardia in CVID, and (d) Clostridium septicum/malignancy are established associations from their respective Mandell chapters, not the Capnocytophaga chapter.

cohort_answer.text: 1) Capnocytophaga canimorsus. 2) Aeromonas. Others: Burkholderia, Edwardsiella, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas. Salt water: Vibrio, Shewanella, Erysipelothrix. 3) Giardia. 4) Clostridium septicum (w/o trauma), due to the malignancy

questions.model_answer:
a) Clostridium septicum (neutropenic sepsis with gas-gangrene-like bullae; strong association with GI malignancy and leukemia).
b) Giardia lamblia (Giardia duodenalis) - classic cause of chronic diarrhea/bloating in CVID.
c) Streptococcus pneumoniae - the leading cause of overwhelming postsplenectomy sepsis among encapsulated organisms (also Hib and Neisseria meningitidis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Clostridium septicum (part a) and Giardia in CVID (part b) are not from this chapter; standard ID knowledge (Mandell Clostridium and CVID chapters).

cohort_answer.text: AML case: Clostridium septicum. CVID: Giardia lamblia. Asplenic: Pneumococcal sepsis; Meningococcal sepsis; Salmonella; Capnocytophaga; H. influenzae. Freshwater swimmer: Aeromonas spp.

questions.question: In common variable immunodeficiency, name the organism causing GI discomfort, bloating and diarrhea, and list the infections these patients are at risk for.

parts.text: CVID patient with GI discomfort, bloating and diarrhea: name the organism.
Infections that CVID patients are at risk for.

parts_raw.text: CVID patient with GI discomfort, bloating and diarrhea? (organism)
Infections at risk in CVID

questions.model_answer: a) Giardia lamblia (Giardia duodenalis). b) Predominantly encapsulated/extracellular bacterial infections from defective humoral immunity: recurrent sinopulmonary infection (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) with bronchiectasis; otitis/sinusitis; GI infection and chronic enteropathy (Giardia, norovirus with chronic diarrhea, Campylobacter, Salmonella); Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma (joints, GU); and bacterial sepsis with encapsulated organisms. Chronic norovirus is a recognised cause of enteropathy in CVID.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the CVID-norovirus enteropathy link is in Ch. 305 (p. 3625); Giardia and the fuller infection spectrum are from Mandell PID chapters.

cohort_answer.text: A) Giardia lamblia. B) Pulmonary: H influenzae, S. pneumo, Staph, Mycoplasma, enterovirus (chronic lung disease: bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis with granulomas, acute/chronic bronchitis). H&N: rhinosinusitis, otitis media, conjunctivitis. GI: acute infectious diarrhea (norovirus, Campylobacter, cryptosporidium, Giardia, Salmonella, H pylori, IBD). UTI: mycoplasma/ureaplasma. Joints: septic arthritis. Skin: herpes zoster, molluscum. CNS: meningitis. Systemic: bacterial sepsis especially encapsulated organisms.
